title: A path integral is little arrows joined head to tail
text: When Feynman explained quantum electrodynamics he tried not to start with complex analysis. His device was to give every possible path a little stopwatch: the time a photon takes along that path sets the angle of the hand. Join all those little arrows head to tail in order, and the square of the length of the final arrow is the probability that the event happens. An integral is just adding those arrows continuously. The name is intimidating; the picture is plain.

title: Calculus is zooming in and slicing, not a formula sheet
text: Feynman disliked calculus taught as a page of derivative rules. A derivative, to him, was putting a curved road under a microscope to see how steep each tiny piece is; an integral was cutting a shape into thin slices and stacking them back up to get the area. The picture comes first; formulas are just the picture written in symbols. Someone who only memorizes formulas freezes when the shape is one they have not seen.

title: Notation is a cane, not a leg
text: In high school Feynman found the textbook's trigonometric notation easy to misread, so he invented his own symbols with little hooks. With his notation some identities became obvious at a glance. His conclusion was not that his symbols were superior, but that notation is a cane people build for convenience: if it fits badly, carve another one. Treating the cane as a leg is what really leaves you unable to walk.

title: Erasing one bit costs a little heat
text: In the Lectures on Computation Feynman chased a very plain question: why does a computer get hot? Part of the answer is not wire resistance but the computation itself. An ordinary AND gate squeezes two inputs into one output, and the original inputs can never be recovered. Erasing one bit is like pouring two cups of water into one basin: irreversible, and it costs entropy and heat. Reversible computing starts from not throwing the information away, so the computation can be run backwards.

title: To simulate nature, build a machine that follows nature's rules
text: Simulating a few dozen interacting quantum particles on a classical computer blows up the state space; memory gives out first. Feynman's 1981 intuition was direct: the world at bottom does not run on classical billiard-ball rules, so forcing a classical machine to simulate it is like chasing light with an abacus. The natural way to simulate a quantum world is to build a computer that itself runs on quantum rules.

title: There is plenty of room at the bottom
text: In 1959 Feynman asked a question that sounded like a joke: why can't the whole Encyclopaedia Britannica be written on the head of a pin? The laws of physics do not forbid it. He added that nature packs an enormous amount of genetic information into a single cell, and that people would eventually build tiny machines able to crawl into blood vessels like surgeons. Nanotechnology largely began as a path out of that question.

title: A license plate miracle is a target drawn afterwards
text: In a parking lot Feynman saw a license plate and exclaimed: with millions of cars in the state, what were the odds I would run into exactly this string? Then he demolished his own wonder. Any plate sitting there has an equally tiny probability. Seeing where the arrow landed and then drawing the bullseye around it is not a miracle; it is a statistical illusion. The real question is: what did I predict before I saw the result?

title: Mental cube roots run on approximation, not brute force
text: In Brazil Feynman raced an abacus expert to find the cube root of 1729.03. While the other man was still moving beads, he had already said about 12.002. The trick was plain: 1728 is exactly 12 cubed, and the extra 1.03 is only a crumb; a first-order linear approximation gives the first few decimals. He did not try to produce every digit. He grabbed the order of magnitude and the leading term first, and the remaining error was too small to change the answer.
